explanations.explanation: Ramoth-gilead is the city. In Samaria, Ahab sacrificed many sheep and cattle for Jehoshaphat and the people with him, and urged him to march up to Ramoth-gilead (2 Chronicles 18:2). That's a big welcome with a big ask, friend.

Jericho is a famous city, so I get why it jumped out. But Ahab isn't pointing at Jericho here. The text says he urged Jehoshaphat to march up to Ramoth-gilead (2 Chronicles 18:2). Nice guess, different city.

Nineveh is a big name in the Bible, so it makes sense that it popped into your head. This passage isn't about Nineveh, though. Ahab urges Jehoshaphat to march up to Ramoth-gilead (2 Chronicles 18:2). Different city, different road trip.

I see why you'd think Judah would sit this one out. But Jehoshaphat says the opposite: "I am as you are, and my people are your people; we will join you in the war." That's a full yes, with his people thrown in. He's all in, friend.

Right, because Judah isn't staying out of it. Jehoshaphat tells Ahab, "I am as you are, and my people are your people; we will join you in the war." He doesn't just say yes for himself, he puts his whole people in the boat. That's a big promise to make in one breath.
Jehoshaphat says, "Please inquire first for the word of the LORD." He wants to hear from God before anybody marches anywhere. Smart move, friend.
An angel isn't what Jehoshaphat asks for. He says, "Please inquire first for the word of the LORD." He asks for God's word, plain and simple. Good guess, though, friend.

The army is the thing they're already getting ready to use, so I see the mix-up. But Jehoshaphat asks Ahab to "…inquire first for the word of the LORD." He wants to hear from God before the army moves an inch. First the word, then the marching.
Nope, the prophets say the exact opposite. They tell Ahab, "Go up," and add that "…God will deliver it into the hand of the king." Four hundred men, one answer. That's a LOT of yes.
Right. All four hundred say "Go up," and promise that "…God will deliver it into the hand of the king." Not one of them says to hold back. That's the whole room nodding together.

explanations.answer: He never prophesies anything good for Ahab
explanations.explanation: That's what Ahab says himself: "…I hate him because he never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad." Notice that Ahab's complaint isn't that Micaiah gets it wrong. It's that he doesn't like what he hears. That's a tough way to shop for advice.

explanations.answer: He refuses to come whenever Ahab calls
explanations.explanation: That sounds believable, but it's not what Ahab says. His reason is this: "…I hate him because he never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad." Nothing about Micaiah ignoring a call. In fact, Ahab sends for him and he comes.

explanations.answer: He once insulted Ahab in front of Israel
explanations.explanation: A public insult would explain a grudge, I'll give you that. But the text doesn't say that. Ahab's reason is that Micaiah "…never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad." His problem is the message, not a scene in front of the crowd.
Yes. When Ahab says he hates Micaiah, Jehoshaphat answers, "The king should not say that!" He doesn't let it slide, even though he's the guest. I'd say that takes some nerve, friend.
Jehoshaphat does speak up. After Ahab says he hates Micaiah, Jehoshaphat answers, "The king should not say that!" He's a guest at Ahab's table, and he still says it. I think that took guts.

Iron horns, made for himself. Zedekiah then declares, "With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off." The man showed up with an accessory, friend. I stamp cookies, and even I never brought a prop.

A bronze serpent is in the Bible, in Numbers 21:9, but not here. Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made iron horns for himself (2 Chronicles 18:10). He said they'd gore the Arameans. Different metal, different animal.

A yoke is a good guess for a prophet's prop, but that's not what's in this passage. Zedekiah made iron horns for himself and said, "With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off." Horns, not a yoke. Iron, not wood.

explanations.answer: Speak favorably like the other prophets
explanations.explanation: That's the coaching. The messenger says the prophets all agree in favor of the king, so "…please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably." It's a friendly nudge to go along with the crowd. Sounds easy, until you're the one in the room.

explanations.answer: Stay silent in front of the kings
explanations.explanation: Silence is not what the messenger asks for. He wants Micaiah to talk, and to say what the others said: "…let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably." The request is to match the crowd, not to go quiet.

explanations.answer: Tell Ahab to wait another year
explanations.explanation: Waiting a year would be a different request entirely. The messenger says, "…let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably." He wants Micaiah to join the chorus. No calendar involved.

Micaiah says, "As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever my God tells me." The messenger had just told him the prophets were speaking favorably to the king, and asked him to speak favorably too (2 Chronicles 18:12). Micaiah's words are going to come from his God, friend.

The messenger did ask him to speak favorably like the prophets, so I get the guess. But Micaiah says, "…I will speak whatever my God tells me." He doesn't say he'll speak what the king says. He starts with an oath, too.

The messenger just gave him a little coaching, so it's a fair guess. But Micaiah answers, "As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever my God tells me." What he speaks comes from God, not from the messenger.

Yes, and it's a surprise. Micaiah says, "Go up and triumph…" and adds, "for they will be delivered into your hand." That's the same song the four hundred sang. Hold onto that, friend, because Ahab's about to notice something.

It does sound the same, and that's the twist. Micaiah says, "Go up and triumph, for they will be delivered into your hand." That's right in step with the four hundred. What happens next is where he parts ways with them.

explanations.answer: Scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd
explanations.explanation: Micaiah says, "I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd." That's the picture he gives. It's a hard one, and I think Ahab felt it.

explanations.answer: Marching home with the spoils of the city
explanations.explanation: That picture would be a victory parade, and Micaiah's isn't one. He says, "I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd." Scattered on the hills, not marching home.

explanations.answer: Standing guard along the walls of Samaria
explanations.explanation: Standing guard along the walls is a different picture from Micaiah's. He says, "I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd." Israel is scattered on the hills, not standing along the walls of Samaria.
Yes, that's what he says. Micaiah tells what he saw: "And the LORD said, ‘These people have no master; let each one return home in peace.’…" Notice the last part. Home, in peace.
It's true, actually. Micaiah says the LORD said, "These people have no master; let each one return home in peace." It's a quiet line after a scattered picture, friend. Easy to skim past.
The word is "fall." The LORD asks, "Who will entice Ahab king of Israel to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?" Micaiah is describing Ahab's fall, not his victory. That's a heavy one.

I get it, and I bet "win" is what Ahab is hoping for. But the vision says, "Who will entice Ahab king of Israel to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?" The word is "fall." That's the opposite of what the four hundred promised.
"Camp" sounds like a plain army word, so I see the pull. The vision actually says, "…to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?" Ahab marches up, and it doesn't end with a campfire.
The spirit says, "I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets." The word is lying. It's a strange scene, friend, and Micaiah tells it plainly.
A warning spirit would be a kindness, so I see why it's tempting. But the spirit says, "I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets." Lying, not warning.
A guiding spirit would help somebody find the way. This one does the reverse. It says, "I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets." Lying, friend.

explanations.answer: Which way the Spirit of the LORD went to reach Micaiah
explanations.explanation: Zedekiah strikes Micaiah in the face and demands, "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go when He departed from me to speak with you?" He's claiming the Spirit was with him first. It's a hard moment, and I think it hurts to read.

explanations.answer: Who gave Micaiah the right to speak to the king
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a fair thing to snap, but it's not what he says. Zedekiah demands, "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go when He departed from me to speak with you?" His question is about the Spirit of the LORD, and which way He went.

explanations.answer: Why Micaiah dared to stand before the two kings
explanations.explanation: Plenty of people might ask that, but the text doesn't have Zedekiah say it. He demands, "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go when He departed from me to speak with you?" His question is about the Spirit of the LORD.
Micaiah says, "You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room." Notice who Micaiah says will be hiding. It's the man who just struck him, and Micaiah answers with words.

Caves show up all over the Bible, so it's an easy guess. But Micaiah says, "You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room." An inner room, friend. Somewhere inside, tucked away.
A roof is out in the open, and that's not the picture. Micaiah says, "You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room." The hiding place is indoors, tucked away.
Ahab orders, "Put this man in prison and feed him only bread and water until I return safely." Only bread and water, friend. That's the bare minimum, not a well-fed wait.
Right. Ahab says to "…feed him only bread and water until I return safely." Only bread and water. After the feast Ahab threw for Jehoshaphat, that's quite the difference.

explanations.answer: If you return safely the LORD has not spoken through me
explanations.explanation: Micaiah says, "If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me." He puts everything on the line. If Ahab comes home fine, Micaiah is wrong, and he says so out loud.

explanations.answer: You will return safely but your army will not
explanations.explanation: That's a neat twist, but Micaiah doesn't say it. His words are, "If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me." He never promises Ahab a safe trip home. He says that if it happens, he's been wrong.

explanations.answer: The LORD will bring you home before evening
explanations.explanation: That would be a comfort, and it's not what Micaiah gives. He says, "If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me." No promise of getting home, friend. He says that if Ahab returns safely, the LORD has not spoken through him.

explanations.answer: I'll disguise myself and you wear your royal robes
explanations.explanation: Ahab says, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your royal robes." Think about that, friend. He hides, and his guest stands out in the royal robes.

explanations.answer: You lead the charge while I guard the camp
explanations.explanation: That's a different plan, and Ahab doesn't say it. He says, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your royal robes." Ahab goes into the battle too. He just does it in disguise.

explanations.answer: We'll both disguise ourselves as common soldiers
explanations.explanation: It'd be fairer if they both blended in, wouldn't it? But Ahab says, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your royal robes." Only one of them is in disguise, and it's Ahab.

The king of Aram orders his chariot commanders, "Do not fight with anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel." Aram was the nation Ahab was fighting. Only one target on the list, and that's Ahab's crown.
Jehoshaphat is the king of Judah, so I see why it came to mind. But the order was, "Do not fight with anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel." That's Ahab's title, not Jehoshaphat's.

Egypt shows up a lot in Scripture, but it's not in this order. The king of Aram says, "Do not fight with anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel." His eyes are on one king, and he isn't from Egypt.

explanations.answer: He cries out and the LORD helps him
explanations.explanation: The text says, "…Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him. God drew them away from him." He's in the royal robes with chariots turning toward him, and he cries out. That's a good thing to do when you're in trouble, friend.

explanations.answer: He throws off his royal robes and runs
explanations.explanation: That's what I'd probably do, friend. But the text says Jehoshaphat "…cried out, and the LORD helped him." Nothing about throwing off his robes or running. God drew them away from him.

explanations.answer: He hides behind the chariot of Ahab
explanations.explanation: Hiding sounds sensible with chariots coming. But the text says Jehoshaphat "…cried out, and the LORD helped him." There's no hiding place in the story. God drew the commanders away from him.

They don't keep chasing. When the commanders saw that he was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him. It's like thinking you've found your friend in a crowd, then it's a stranger. Time to turn around.
Right. The commanders "…saw that he was not the king of Israel…" and "…they turned back from pursuing him." Wrong king, case closed. They had one target, and it wasn't Jehoshaphat.

explanations.answer: Turn around and take me out of the battle
explanations.explanation: Ahab says to his charioteer, "Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am badly wounded!" The arrow hit between the joints of his armor. Friend, even a disguise couldn't hide him from that.

explanations.answer: Drive me straight toward the king of Aram
explanations.explanation: That would be bold, but it's not what Ahab says. He tells his charioteer, "Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am badly wounded!" He wants out, not a showdown.

explanations.answer: Go find Jehoshaphat and bring him here
explanations.explanation: Jehoshaphat is Ahab's ally, so it's a fair guess. But Ahab says, "Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am badly wounded!" He's thinking about getting out, not calling anyone over.
Yes. The text says, "…at sunset he died." That's the end of Ahab, and it's a sobering line. I think this one is heavy, friend.
I wish it were different, but the text is plain. The king of Israel propped himself up in his chariot until evening, and "…at sunset he died." It's a heavy ending, friend. Micaiah's words stood.
